title: Variables
objective: Declare, name, and reassign variables correctly with let and const.

sourceAlignment.title: JavaScript Crash Course
sourceAlignment.author: Nick Morgan
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: A variable is a named container for a value. You create one with let or const: the keyword, then a name, then an equals sign, then the value. const means the name can never be reassigned after it's set; let means it can. Prefer const by default, and only reach for let when you know the value needs to change later.

Variable names can use letters, digits, underscores, and dollar signs, but can't start with a digit and can't contain spaces. Names are case-sensitive, so score and Score are two different variables. Avoid words JavaScript already uses for something else, like let or function.

Using a name that was never declared with let, const, or var raises a ReferenceError the moment JavaScript tries to read it — this almost always means a typo, or code that runs before the variable was created.
explanation.rule: Use const by default; switch to let only when a variable's value genuinely needs to change later.

examples.title: Declaring and Reassigning
examples.note: forgeName can never be reassigned since it's const. temperature can change since it's let.

checks.question: const count = 5; count = 6; — what happens?
options: A TypeError is thrown, because const can't be reassigned.
A SyntaxError is thrown before the code even runs.

feedback.correct: Correct — reassigning a const variable throws a TypeError at runtime.
feedback.incorrect: const variables can't be reassigned after their initial value is set — doing so throws a TypeError.

assignment.title: Forge Temperature
assignment.brief: Write reportTemperature() that stores 1200 in a variable and logs that variable.
requirements: Store 1200 in a variable using const or let.
Log that variable, not the literal number directly.

hints: Declare a variable with const temperature = 1200;
console.log(temperature) logs the variable's value, not the word "temperature".
You don't need let here since the value never changes — const works fine.
The output should be exactly the number 1200 on its own line.
